title: Lissajous Figures
short_intro: Lissajous figures are the resultant geometric patterns formed by the superposition of two harmonic oscillations acting at right angles to each other. They provide a precise graphical method for comparing frequencies, phase differences, and amplitudes of orthogonal vibrations.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Understanding the graphical shapes formed for frequency ratios of 1:1 and 1:2 with various phase differences, and identification of straight lines, ellipses, and circles.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: General parametric equations, analytical determination of frequency ratios using tangent counting methods, phase angle determination from axial intercepts, and applications in cathode-ray oscilloscopes.

prerequisites: Trigonometric identities for multiple and compound angles

concept_notes.heading: Definition and Principle of Superposition
bullets: Lissajous figures are formed when a particle is subjected simultaneously to two mutually perpendicular simple harmonic motions.
Let the motions be along the X-axis and Y-axis with frequencies ω<sub>x</sub> and ω<sub>y</sub> respectively.
The resultant trajectory traced by the particle in the X-Y plane depends on the amplitude ratio, frequency ratio, and initial phase difference.

concept_notes.heading: Case of Equal Frequencies (ω<sub>x</sub> = ω<sub>y</sub> = ω)
bullets: When the frequencies are equal, the general path is an ellipse inscribed in a rectangle of sides 2a and 2b, where a and b are the amplitudes.
When the phase difference δ = 0 or π, the trajectory degenerates into a straight line sloping upwards or downwards.
When δ = π/2 or 3π/2 and amplitudes are equal (a = b), the ellipse becomes a circle.

concept_notes.heading: Case of Harmonic Frequencies (ω<sub>y</sub> / ω<sub>x</sub> = n / m)
bullets: When the frequencies are in the ratio of small integers, closed open curves or loops are formed.
The number of horizontal loops equals the frequency of the Y-vibration, and the number of vertical loops equals the frequency of the X-vibration.
Tangents drawn to the curve parallel to the X-axis and Y-axis help determine the frequency ratio by the intersection method.

concept_notes.heading: Experimental Determination using Cathode-Ray Oscilloscope (CRO)
bullets: A CRO can display Lissajous figures when sinusoidal signals are applied to the X-plates and Y-plates simultaneously.
By adjusting the frequency of a standard oscillator on one channel, unknown frequencies can be measured accurately.
A stationary, non-rotating pattern confirms a precise rational integer ratio between the two applied frequencies.

derivations.title: Derivation of the General Cartesian Equation for Equal Frequencies
derivations.conditions: Two mutually perpendicular SHMs with equal frequency ω and phase difference δ.
steps: Write the displacement equations: x = a sin(ωt) and y = b sin(ωt + δ).
Expand the second equation: y = b [sin(ωt)cos(δ) + cos(ωt)sin(δ)].
Substitute sin(ωt) = x/a and cos(ωt) = ±√(1 - x<sup>2</sup>/a<sup>2</sup>) into the expanded equation.
Rearrange terms to isolate the radical: y - (x/a)b cos(δ) = b ±√(1 - x<sup>2</sup>/a<sup>2</sup>) sin(δ).
Square both sides and simplify to obtain the general equation of an ellipse: (x<sup>2</sup>/a<sup>2</sup>) + (y<sup>2</sup>/b<sup>2</sup>) - (2xy/ab)cos(δ) = sin<sup>2</sup>(δ).

derivations.title: Determination of Phase Difference from Axial Intercepts
derivations.conditions: Equal frequencies (ωx = ωy), elliptical trace with axes inclined to coordinate axes.
steps: Consider the equation of the ellipse when x = 0; the Y-intercept is given by y<sub>0</sub> = ± b sin(δ).
Consider the maximum amplitude along the Y-axis, which is y<sub>max</sub> = b when sin(ωt + δ) = 1.
Take the ratio of the intercept to the maximum amplitude: y<sub>0</sub> / y<sub>max</sub> = [b sin(δ)] / b = sin(δ).
Calculate the phase difference using the inverse sine function: δ = sin<sup>-1</sup>(y<sub>0</sub> / y<sub>max</sub>).

formula_sheet.name: General displacement along X
formula_sheet.variables: a = amplitude of X-motion, ω<sub>x</sub> = angular frequency, t = time

formula_sheet.name: General displacement along Y
formula_sheet.variables: b = amplitude of Y-motion, δ = phase difference

formula_sheet.name: Frequency ratio from tangent counts
formula_sheet.variables: N<sub>x</sub> = number of tangents touching the top/bottom, N<sub>y</sub> = number of tangents touching the sides

formula_sheet.name: Phase angle via intercepts
formula_sheet.variables: y<sub>(x=0)</sub> = intercept on Y-axis, y<sub>max</sub> = peak Y amplitude

formula_sheet.name: Tangent of orientation angle for principal axes
formula_sheet.variables: θ = angle of tilt of ellipse axes with coordinate axes

graphs_and_experiments.title: Lissajous Figure for δ = 0 (ω<sub>x</sub> = ω<sub>y</sub>)
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A straight line passing through the origin with a positive slope y = (b/a)x.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The two orthogonal oscillations are completely in phase, resulting in rectilinear motion.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Direct question in TGT on identifying phase difference from a linear trace.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Lissajous Figure for δ = π/2, a = b (ω<sub>x</sub> = ω<sub>y</sub>)
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A perfect circle inscribed in a square of side 2a.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Equal amplitudes and a phase difference of π/2 create uniform circular motion.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Frequently asked PGT condition for obtaining circular polarization or circular Lissajous figures.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Lissajous Figure for Frequency Ratio 1:2
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A figure-eight (or parabola-like looped curve) enclosed in a rectangular box with 1 horizontal tangent and 2 vertical tangents.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The frequency of the vertical oscillation is twice that of the horizontal oscillation (ω<sub>y</sub> = 2ω<sub>x</sub>).
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Standard diagram-based question for PGT to test frequency ratio identification.

solved_numericals.question: Two perpendicular SHMs are given by x = 3 sin(ωt) and y = 3 sin(ωt + π/2). What is the resulting Lissajous figure?
solution_steps: Identify the amplitudes: a = 3 and b = 3.
Since amplitudes are equal and phase difference is π/2, the equation x<sup>2</sup> + y<sup>2</sup> = a<sup>2</sup> represents a circle.

solved_numericals.question: A Lissajous figure formed by two orthogonal SHMs has 3 horizontal tangents and 2 vertical tangents. What is the frequency ratio ω<sub>y</sub> / ω<sub>x</sub>?
solution_steps: Recall the relation between frequency ratio and number of tangents: ω<sub>y</sub> / ω<sub>x</sub> = N<sub>x</sub> / N<sub>y</sub>.
Here, N<sub>x</sub> (number of intersections or tangents touching horizontal boundaries / parallel to X-axis) = 3.
N<sub>y</sub> (number of tangents touching vertical boundaries / parallel to Y-axis) = 2.

solved_numericals.question: An elliptical Lissajous figure with equal amplitudes a = b has a Y-intercept of 2 cm and a maximum Y-amplitude of 4 cm. Calculate the phase difference δ.
solution_steps: Use the formula relating phase difference to intercepts: sin(δ) = y<sub>0</sub> / y<sub>max</sub>.
Determine the angle: δ = sin<sup>-1</sup>(0.5) = π/6 radians (30°) or 5π/6 radians (150°).

assumptions_and_limitations: Assumes the orthogonal harmonic motions have constant amplitudes and stable frequencies over the observation interval.
Limitations include difficulty in resolving complex ratios when frequency drifts occur or when harmonic distortion is present in the input signals.

common_misconceptions.wrong: A straight-line Lissajous figure always means the phase difference is zero.
common_misconceptions.correct: A straight line is obtained whenever the phase difference is an integral multiple of π (δ = nπ), which includes both 0 and π.
common_misconceptions.why: When δ = π, the slope of the line is negative, whereas for δ = 0, the slope is positive.

common_misconceptions.wrong: The number of loops in a Lissajous figure directly equals the frequency of the wave.
common_misconceptions.correct: The number of loops gives the ratio of the frequencies along the two axes, not the absolute frequency values.
common_misconceptions.why: Counting horizontal and vertical tangents yields only the relative integer ratio N<sub>x</sub>:N<sub>y</sub> = ω<sub>y</sub>:ω<sub>x</sub>.

quick_revision: Equal frequencies with δ = 0 or π give straight lines; δ = π/2 with equal amplitudes gives a circle.
General displacement along X: x = a \sin(\omega_x t)
General displacement along Y: y = b \sin(\omega_y t + \delta)
